summary: Documents a method used by cisco for sending X.25 packets over IP networks by encapsulating the X.25 packet level in TCP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Packets from an old network style are put inside envelopes of another style so they can travel across the Internet.

subtitle: Sending X.25 packets over the Internet using TCP.

tldr.problem: X.25 is a packet-level protocol used in older networks, but organizations need to transport X.25 traffic over IP internets.
tldr.mechanism: XOT encapsulates X.25 packets inside TCP packets, adding a small 4-byte header with version and length information to mark packet boundaries in the TCP stream.
tldr.outcome: Devices can exchange X.25 traffic over IP networks while keeping standard X.25 protocol operation intact, allowing legacy networks to connect through modern infrastructure.

today: RFC 1613 is an Informational RFC published in May 1994. It documents XOT, a method initially developed by cisco Systems for encapsulating X.25 over TCP/IP. As a technical specification, it remains valid for implementations that need to transport legacy X.25 traffic over modern IP networks.

sections.title: X.25 Transport Problem
sections.content:
X.25 is a packet-level protocol that requires a reliable link layer below it. Historically it ran over LAPB (a link-level protocol). The RFC documents a way to send X.25 packets over IP internets by encapsulating the X.25 Packet Level inside TCP packets.

TCP provides a reliable byte stream, but X.25 needs message semantics—it requires clear boundaries between packets. XOT solves this with a small 4-byte header between TCP and X.25 that includes a length field. This length field separates X.25 packets within the TCP stream while preserving all normal X.25 protocol rules and state transitions.
sections.plainLanguage: X.25 is an old way to send messages. It needs a special carrier below it. The Internet has TCP, which is newer. To make them work together, you wrap X.25 messages in a tiny label that says how big each message is.

sections.title: Packet Structure
sections.content:
Each XOT packet consists of an IP header, then a TCP header, then a 4-byte XOT header, then the X.25 packet. The XOT header contains two 16-bit fields: a Version field (which must be 0) and a Length field that specifies the size of the X.25 packet in bytes.

If the Version field contains any value other than 0, the TCP connection must be closed. If the Length field has an illegal value (not a valid X.25 packet length), the TCP connection must also be closed. This strict version checking ensures compatibility across implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapper has four key parts: two numbers saying what version this is (must be zero), and two numbers saying how many bytes the X.25 message is. The receiver reads the size and knows exactly where the message ends.

sections.title: TCP Connection and Virtual Circuits
sections.content:
All XOT connections use TCP port 1998, an IANA Registered Port designated for XOT by cisco Systems. A separate TCP connection must be established for each X.25 virtual circuit. The TCP connection is created before the virtual circuit can be set up, and data must not be sent with the TCP SYN packet.

Once the TCP connection is established, the initiating XOT sends an X.25 Call packet. The connection receives either a Call Confirm packet (accepting the call) or a Clear packet (rejecting it). After clearing a virtual circuit, the TCP connection may be maintained for reuse or closed immediately.
sections.plainLanguage: To connect, you open a door (TCP connection) to port 1998 on the other computer. Each conversation (virtual circuit) gets its own door. Once the door opens, you send your request through it.

sections.title: Packet Handling and Flow Control
sections.content:
When forwarding X.25 packets across an XOT connection, implementations must modify the logical channel number (LCN) field to match the outgoing X.25 interface, but should not modify other packet header information unless required for proper X.25 operation. The specification supports both end-to-end and local flow control approaches.

For implementations supporting different flow control modulos on each side, the XOT layer may modify the X.25 General Format Identifier to match the local interface requirements. Interrupt, Reset, and Reset Confirm packets are sent over the TCP connection using normal X.25 formats, maintaining their end-to-end semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: As messages travel through the door, the post office (XOT) updates the address labels to match the local post office system. It keeps track of what size messages each end can handle and makes sure they don't overwhelm each other.

sections.title: Permanent Virtual Circuits
sections.content:
XOT may also support Permanent Virtual Circuits (PVCs), which are pre-established connections that do not require call setup. PVC setup uses a non-standard X.25 packet type (0xF5) sent immediately after the TCP connection is established. This packet includes version information, status codes, interface names, logical channel numbers, and flow control parameters from both sides of the connection.

The initiator sends a PVC setup packet with status 0x00. If the responder agrees, it returns status 0x00, and the PVC is established. If setup fails, the responder returns an error status code indicating the reason (such as configuration mismatch or incompatible flow control values). Once a PVC is successfully established, both ends complete a Reset procedure on their local interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: For permanent connections that don't need a hello first, you can set them up directly. Both sides exchange special setup messages with their names, door numbers, and sizes they can handle. If they match, the permanent line is ready to use.
